clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of dopamine synthesis caused by TH mutations, in which tyrosine hydroxylase fails to convert tyrosine to L-dopa, reducing dopamine and downstream noradrenaline/adrenaline
It is an important treatable cause of a levodopa-responsive movement disorder, and a therapeutic trial of levodopa is central to both diagnosis and management
Presentations range from a milder infantile-onset dopa-responsive dystonia/parkinsonism to a severe early-onset encephalopathy with hypokinesia, oculogyric crises, ptosis, and autonomic features

The biochemical signature in cerebrospinal fluid is low homovanillic acid (a dopamine metabolite) with a normal 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (serotonin metabolite) and normal pterins, distinguishing it from biopterin defects
Because pterin metabolism is intact, blood phenylalanine and pterin profiles are normal, contrasting with tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) disorders
Some patients, particularly the severe phenotype, respond only partially to levodopa and require careful, gradual dose titration to avoid dyskinesia and irritability
reference.pathophysiology: Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyses the rate-limiting, tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent conversion of tyrosine to L-dopa, the precursor of dopamine and, in turn, noradrenaline and adrenaline. Biallelic TH mutations reduce enzyme activity, causing a central deficiency of catecholaminergic neurotransmission. Dopaminergic hypofunction produces the extrapyramidal features (dystonia, parkinsonism, hypokinesia, oculogyric crises), while reduced noradrenergic and adrenergic signalling contributes to ptosis, autonomic instability, and, in severe cases, encephalopathy. Because the pterin cofactor pathway is unaffected, phenylalanine handling and pterin concentrations remain normal, and the CSF shows selectively low dopamine metabolites.
additionalDifferentials: GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency (autosomal dominant dopa-responsive/Segawa dystonia)
Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis/recycling defects (PTPS, DHPR, sepiapterin reductase)
Early-onset idiopathic dystonia or juvenile parkinsonism
additionalInvestigations: Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites showing low homovanillic acid with normal 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid
CSF pterins (biopterin and neopterin) to confirm a normal pterin profile
TH gene sequencing to confirm the molecular diagnosis
Plasma phenylalanine (normal) to distinguish from BH4 disorders detected on newborn screening
Documented clinical and biochemical response to a levodopa trial
Brain MRI, usually unremarkable, to exclude structural causes of the movement disorder
redFlags: Severe neonatal or infantile hypokinetic-rigid encephalopathy with autonomic instability
Recurrent oculogyric crises causing distress and feeding difficulty
Failure to consider a treatable dopa-responsive disorder in a child labelled as cerebral palsy
Marked levodopa-induced dyskinesia or behavioural disturbance during titration
reference.prognosis: The milder dopa-responsive phenotype often improves markedly and durably with levodopa and BH4-independent dopaminergic therapy, whereas the severe encephalopathic form responds less completely and may leave residual disability. Early recognition and treatment improve motor and developmental outcomes.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by not offering a levodopa trial in an unexplained childhood movement disorder
Starting levodopa at too high a dose and provoking dyskinesia, irritability, or dystonic storms
Confusing the disorder with BH4 defects, which additionally require cofactor and sometimes serotonin-precursor therapy
Overlooking autonomic and ptosis features that reflect noradrenergic deficiency
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
management: Levodopa combined with a peripheral dopa decarboxylase inhibitor as the mainstay, replacing the deficient dopamine that tyrosine hydroxylase can no longer synthesise
Cautious, gradual dose titration, particularly in the severe phenotype, to achieve motor benefit while avoiding dyskinesia and irritability
Adjunctive dopaminergic agents such as dopamine agonists, and anticholinergics where dystonia persists despite levodopa
Supportive management of oculogyric crises, autonomic instability and feeding difficulty in the encephalopathic form
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and developmental support to optimise motor function and milestones
Multidisciplinary follow-up through paediatric neurology and metabolic medicine
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder with family assessment
